chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Yahya al-Attar (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated, from his father, from Sahl ibn Ziyad al-Adami, from Hamzah ibn Muhammad, who said:
I wrote to Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) asking him about the body and the image, so he wrote in reply: 'Glory be to Him who has nothing whatsoever like unto Him.'

key_terms.أَبُو الْحَسَنِ عَلَيْهِ السَّلَام: Abu al-Hasan (AS) (referring to Imam Musa al-Kadhim)
key_terms.سُبْحَانَ مَنْ لَيْسَ كَمِثْلِهِ شَيْءٌ: Glory be to Him who has nothing whatsoever like unto Him (Quranic affirmation of divine transcendence)

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic theological understanding of Allah's body and form according to the Imams?
ai.summary: In this concise narration from Shaykh al-Saduq’s *al-Tawhid*, Imam al-Rida (AS) responds to a query on divine corporeality (*jism*) and form (*surah*) by citing the Quranic phrase 'Glory be to Him who has nothing whatsoever like unto Him.' This response underscores the Shia doctrine of *tanzih* (divine transcendence), rejecting anthropomorphic attributes and affirming that God is free from physical limitations and spatial containment. The brevity of the answer highlights the sufficiency of this verse in establishing the core principle of divine unity against the *Mujassima* (those who attribute body to God).

en.sayed-ali-raza-rizvi: 17. Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Yahya al-`Attar (may Allah be pleased with him) said, on the authority of his father, on the authority of Sahl ibn Ziyad al-Adami, on the authority of Hamzah ibn Muhammad
that I wrote to Abu al-Hasan al-Kadhim (AS) asking him whether Allah had a body or an image. Hence he (AS) wrote in reply: “Glory be to Him who has nothing whatsoever like unto Him,”
